One Activity Is Not Too Much to Ask

When our principal announced that every student would have to join at least one extracurricular activity, the complaints started before the announcement was over. People said they had no time, that school should end at the last bell, that nobody can force you to have fun. I understand those complaints, and I made a few of them myself. But after thinking it through, I agree with the decision. One activity is a small requirement, and what students get out of it is worth far more than the hour or two a week it costs.

The strongest reason is that many students will never try anything unless something pushes them. In sixth grade I signed up for nothing. I went home, did my homework, and watched videos until dinner. In seventh grade my mother made me join the school newspaper because she was tired of seeing me on the couch. I was annoyed for about two weeks. Then I wrote a story about why the cafeteria ran out of pizza every Friday, and people I had never spoken to stopped me in the hall to talk about it. I would not have found out I liked interviewing people if the choice had been left entirely to me. A requirement does for every student what my mother did for me.

Activities also teach things that classes do not. In math class, if I do not do my work, only my grade suffers. On the yearbook staff, if one person misses a deadline, forty pages go to the printer late and everyone pays for it. A student council treasurer has to explain to real classmates why there is not enough money for both a dance and a field day. A goalkeeper who lets in three goals has to show up at practice the next afternoon anyway. These are lessons about depending on other people and having them depend on you, and a worksheet cannot give them.

There is also the matter of belonging. A school of several hundred students can be a lonely place if you only know the people who sit near you. Activities mix students who would never otherwise meet. The chess club at our school has eighth graders teaching sixth graders, and the stage crew includes kids from every lunch table. A student who has even one group to belong to has a reason to come to school on the days when the classes alone are not enough of one.

The objections deserve an answer. Some students truly are busy. They watch younger brothers and sisters, or they have jobs, or they ride a bus that leaves at 3:10. The principal should take this seriously, and the rule should be flexible enough to handle it. Some clubs could meet during lunch or the advisory period. A student who already plays in a town soccer league or volunteers at a church should be able to count that. With those adjustments, the requirement asks for very little: one activity, chosen by the student, out of dozens.

Others say that forcing students takes the fun away. I think this gets it backward. Nobody is being assigned to the debate team against their will. The student still chooses, and the list is wide enough to include robotics, art club, track, the literary magazine, and the garden committee. If nothing on the list fits, students can propose something new, which is how our school ended up with a cooking club.

School is supposed to prepare us for more than tests. It is supposed to help us figure out what we are good at and how to work with other people. Requiring one activity makes sure that every student, not just the confident ones, gets that chance. I started seventh grade resenting the push I was given. I am glad now that somebody gave it.
